Okay. Can you hear me alright? Okay, great. Good afternoon, Chair Hanif and members of the committee. Thank you for the first ever opportunity to testify today at the Fiscal Year Budget for the Mayor’s Office of People with Disabilities. My name is Nisha Agarwal, and I have short black hair and brown skin. I’m wearing a black top and black trousers and a multicolor necklace. I have aphasia and I have my handy cane at my side. I am honored to serve as the Commissioner of the Mayor’s Office for People with Disabilities, also known as MOPD, also known as MOPD. First, I will share about the role of MOPD. MOPD’s mission is to ensure that New York City is accessible and inclusive for the more than one million New Yorkers with disabilities who live and work in our city. We believe that accessibility is not limited to one program or one agency. It is a citywide responsibility. MOPD’s work closely– works closely with partners across government and external stakeholders to ensure that policies, services and

programs consider the needs of New Yorkers with disabilities from the start. I want to be– I would like to share the vision for MOPD under the leadership of Mayor Mamdani, but to understand the importance of this work, it is helpful to look at some of the challenges faced on New Yorkers with disabilities. In employment, for example, just 40 percent of New Yorkers with disabilities of working age are employed, compared to 73 percent of the city’s overall working age population. And for those who are in the labor force, the unemployment is nearly double, 13 percent of people with disabilities compared with seven percent citywide. In education, almost 30 percent of adult New Yorkers with disabilities receive less than a high school education compared to 16 percent of the city’s overall population, and the opposite is true as well. While over 41 percent of city’s overall population received a bachelor’s degree or higher, only 23 percent of people with disabilities had the same. These inequities persist, not because of lack of skill or motivation, but because of structural barriers, inaccessible practices and limited

awareness of available support. So, recognizing these challenges, MOPD’s vision is to strengthen, partner and expand our services and policies for people with disabilities. I’ll start with the strengths. The key priorities from the Mayor: affordable housing, access to health and mental health, accessible transportation, education equity, and employment opportunities are critical to people with disabilities and to most New Yorkers. Given that, part of our strategy is to strengthen some of the existing work we already have. For example, NYC At Work program does continuing of individual services to both job-seekers and employers. For job-seekers, we offer career advice, resume and individual preparedness, guidance on disclosure, and reasonable accommodations, retention services and support for those who apply for city government. On the employment side, we work with employers on recruitment support, pre-screening candidate referrals and personalizing hiring events, among other things. This has been very successful, but MOPD wants to strengthen and expand NYC At Work by doing digital literacy training or mental health

supports as people with disabilities rebuild confidence and reenter the workforce. There are also administrative hurdles and legal– lengthy approvals for getting a city job. That can discourage both job seekers and the hiring managers. To accomplish this, we need to work with external stakeholders and internal stakeholders, our other city agencies, to do it, and to do it well. We also want to grow and strengthen the systemic change side of this equation. Using policy research and communications strategically, we can start to influence the decision-makers at the city, state and federal level, and have an impact on people with disabilities systemically. To expand our existing programs or to work on new priorities, building and expanding our partnerships is key. So, first I’ll talk about the disability communities. Disability advocates, our trusted community messengers, have deep community ties, and the ability to focus on specific issues in-depth. MOPD covers the range of disability services and accessibility, has convening power and also has access to City Hall and other city agencies. MOPD should be in constant partnership with

disability advocates, working together on our shared priorities. And when we have a disagreement, have an open discussion and next steps for resolution. I will also add that MOPD should also ensure that lesser-known disabilities, for example, language learning and mental health disabilities, should be incorporated into these discussions. Next, our city agencies. Historically, people with disability were brought into– and the end of any project, not at the start. This was frustrating for people with disabilities and it was a disservice to those agencies that were involved in that project, because in the end we chose the faster design instead of the best design. In the new administration, however, the heads of agencies that were chosen including me are into collaboration and problem-solving. And that is really exciting. MOPD is nimble and knowledgeable on accessibility and inclusion for people with disabilities. The agencies have deep expertise in their issues, and can incorporate in accessibility and inclusion into their projects with MOPD assisting. It’s a win/win. It ensures that the city government is efficient and has a whole approach

model. And New Yorkers, people with disabilities and the broader public will recognize that this city works for them. Next would be broader social movements. In the 1960s and 1970s disability advocates were in conversations with the civil rights movement, women’s rights, LGBT rights, immigrant rights and the anti-war movement. Now, in 2026, it feels more fragmented and siloed. It is important to pollinate those seeds again and using MOPD’s convening power to cultivate the interconnectedness that we all do. And finally, elected officials. Everyone including people in elected office have people in disabilities in their lives. It may be themselves, their friends, their neighbors, or their constituencies. MOPD wants to work, with elected, all of you, to share resources and information and overtime build our relationship and partnerships with all of you. MODP’s vision is bold, but doable. Like, New York City, we don’t want to do the bare minimum. We want to be the best in the country, creating innovative ideas that will have a ripple effect on other cities and states. We don’t want to create programs and policies that impact some and exclude

others. The goal for is if it is helpful– it helps us, it can help others, So, we appreciate the Council’s commitment to accessibility and inclusion, and its focus on the needs of New Yorkers with disabilities. We look forward to working with the community members and city agencies to strengthen accessibility across the government. Thank you all for the opportunity to testify today, And I would love to have more– to answer questions from you. Thank you.

Thank you, Commissioner, and congratulations again. I’m super excited and excited really to hear your testimony and your vision about MOPD. And given this is the first inaugural Disabilities Committee, I think we are going to be a power team.
I agree.

Okay. So, you went into this a little bit around the city agency’s partnerships. I want to understand if you believe New York City is currently meeting its legal obligations under the Americans with Disabilities Act across agencies, and if not, where are we falling

short, and what specific investments are needed to come into compliance?

Yeah. So, MOPD provides oversight, guidance, and technical expertise, and we work closely with agencies to ensure compliance with ADA and local laws. While MOPD does not directly– it doesn’t have the direct enforcement authority as of we’re not a regulatory authority, but we play a central role in identifying issues elevating concerns, setting accessible standards, and ensuring that agencies will follow through.
And how are you all assessing whether or not agencies are complying, and what mechanisms do you have to work with the agencies?

Yeah. So, we have Disability Service Facilitators, or DSF. Our agency representatives who are committed to making their city, that city agencies more inclusive. they work with other agencies and services, but with people with disabilities.
